newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Patriotic feeling runs high in Taiwan over isle.
newsitem.headline: Patriotic feeling runs high in Taiwan over isle.

text.p: Angry Taiwan residents formed an alliance on Sunday to protect the Diaoyu islands from Japan and threatened to organise mass protests against what they said was Tokyo's invasion of the uninhabited East China Sea islands.

The move came after Japanese rightists built a makeshift lighthouse on one of the disputed islands, and Japanese coast guard ships in recent days kept several private Taiwanese boats away from the island when they went to dismantle the structure.

"This kind of invasion behaviour, which had suppressed us for almost 100 years, is unbearable," organiser Hsu Li-nung, a retired general and member of Taiwan's opposition New Party, said at the ceremony establishing the new group.
Taiwan was a Japanese colony for 50 years until the end of World War Two.
Taiwan's foreign ministry has formally protested to Japan over the Diaoyu issue, urging Tokyo to use restraint. It has also said it was "delighted" by the show of patriotism at home.

"It is the government's responsibilty to safeguard the Diaoyu islands," legislator Lee Ching-hua, another organiser of the alliance, told journalists. "But we are very disappointed because it allows Japan's invasion to happen again and again."
The Diaoyus, known as the Senkakus in Japanese, are about 300 km (190 miles) west of Japan's Okinawa island and 200 km (125 miles) east of Taiwan. They are claimed by Taipei, Tokyo and Beijing.
Japan's moves to assert sovereignty over the Diaoyus have also angered Chinese in Hong Kong and on the mainland.
Taiwanese media hired private fishing boats to sail to the islands but were expelled by Japanese vessels.
"We should be prepared to fight," one lawmaker told Taiwan's parliament on Friday.
In Hong Hong, more than 3,000 protesters took to the streets on Sunday. "Down with Japanese militarism," they shouted at a rally in a playground where they burned Japanese flags.
Beijing and Tokyo remain deeply divided over their rival claims, but China recently toned down its rhetoric.
Taiwan has no diplomatic ties with Japan, which recognises Beijing's communist government.
The sovereignty dispute warmed up in July when 200 Taiwan fishing boats threatened to sail to one of the Diaoyu islands and tear down the lighthouse built there by the Japan Youth Federation.
The protest was cancelled in August after Japanese officials came to Taiwan to discuss the row and the Japanese group halted plans to further assert Tokyo's claim to the islands.
China had sovereignty over the islands for centuries. Tokyo's claim dates to 1895 when Japan defeated China and seized Taiwan and other territories.
